codex.worst_flaw: The decision to drop rewards uses an absolute digital adoption threshold without requiring evidence that rewards improve verified pre-job completion over plain feedback while preserving safety-check quality.

claude.worst_flaw: The shared crew reward pays everyone once the crew passes a 70% threshold, which invites peer pressure toward rushed or backfilled checks. The only quality check is a five-job weekly sample, too small to reliably catch falsified timestamps or crew-level gaming, and there is no independent shadow validation or replayable event history behind the counts.

holistic.reason: Union-co-designed, usability-first, with fair shared rewards, privacy protections, gaming safeguards and a default-switch for persistence, though a one-hour reward is small and the pilot's reliance on the app fixing real barriers leaves durability uncertain.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward should stay on hold because the quality gate relies on checklist records and has no independent way to detect hazards technicians miss or falsely mark as cleared.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design compares staggered crews for only two weeks with no predefined sample size, uncertainty handling, cost or harm thresholds, and the 10-record weekly audit is too small to reliably detect rushed or backdated checklists across 300 technicians.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, a counting rule that rewards stop-work decisions equally, quality sampling with a pause trigger, a staggered rollout and a clear exit rule make it approvable, but its length and rotating-break reward may be lost on busy technicians, and whether the habit sticks without the reward depends on how much the app friction fixes help.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design uses only a two-week staggered comparison with no stated sample size, uncertainty handling, or predefined cost and harm decision thresholds, and audit history is limited to coordinator corrections without replayable policy versions or a staffed formal appeal route.

codex.worst_flaw: The launch-blocking safety gap is that the audit samples only credited jobs, leaving the pilot unable to detect whether the reward increases unsafe starts on jobs with missing or late checklists.

holistic.reason: It is union-co-designed, rewards an accurate checklist rather than a stopped or started job, protects safety authority, and has a staggered rollout with a pause rule, but a one-hour paid-time-off reward is modest and the app-fixes and default may carry more of the lasting effect than the incentive.

claude.worst_flaw: Both groups' weekly on-time counts are shown to the team and to managers with no small-group or individual-inference protection, and there are no audit details such as replayable policy versions, independent shadow validation or a staffed appeal path beyond the rota owner. Leave and absences are handled only through a backup reviewer, with no rules for excused misses in the personal goal.

codex.worst_flaw: The personal on-time rate counts only PRs engineers pick up, so reviewers can improve their scores by leaving difficult or overdue PRs in the queue.

holistic.reason: It fixes the real bottlenecks first, has clear and fair counting rules, a modest team-lunch reward and a built-in quality check, so sceptical engineers should accept it. The ongoing rules and the four-week reward windows add some complexity, and the weekly sampling is a recurring cost. Lasting change depends on the workflow fixes holding after the reward ends.

codex.worst_flaw: A group can earn the reward through rubber-stamp approvals because submissions receive credit before their quality is verified and payout pauses only when two sampled reviews fail.

claude.worst_flaw: The design gives no rule for leave, on-call or outages, so absent rotation members or uneven per-reviewer load can sink the group's 70% reward threshold, and the comparison uses only two groups over two weeks, too few to separate the reward's effect from noise.

holistic.reason: Fixes the queue first, uses fair measurement, private goals, a team-only view and a quality check, and avoids per-person incentives that sceptical engineers would resent, but the modest reward and extra weekly overhead may leave it unnoticed by some, and it is unclear whether the gains hold without the reward.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design rests on a staggered two-rotation rollout whose two-week overlap is confounded by novelty, rotation differences and shared workflow changes. It sets no harm or cost outcomes in advance and no uncertainty handling, so it cannot show whether the group PTO reward adds anything beyond the queue fixes.

codex.worst_flaw: Both rotations receive the reward during the designated comparison window, so that comparison cannot isolate the reward’s effect beyond the queue changes and private feedback.

holistic.reason: Fixing the queue first, with private feedback, anti-gaming sampling, a team-based half-day reward and a staggered rollout, suits sceptical engineers, but the 80% threshold and the admin burden of PR-history audits may feel heavy, and the reward's effect may fade once the workflow fixes are the only things left.

codex.worst_flaw: The rollout decision relies on a measure that counts a shift as covered after one saved entry, so the pilot can meet its target while most eligible hand-hygiene moments go unlogged.

claude.worst_flaw: Only two monthly audits decide each ward's reward, with no minimum number of observed opportunities, no plan for statistical uncertainty, and no check for nurses behaving differently when they know observers are present, so wards can win or lose on sampling noise while the kiosk logs themselves are never checked against care that actually happened.

holistic.reason: Well-governed, low-burden design with ward-level audit-based rewards, staged rollout, privacy protections and failure checks, but the meal reward is modest and kiosk logging is only loosely tied to the rewarded outcome, so engagement and post-reward persistence are uncertain.

codex.worst_flaw: A ward can earn the meal on as few as 30 verifiable moments even when sampling uncertainty or exclusions concentrated in busy rounds make the apparent improvement unreliable.

claude.worst_flaw: The core outcome is logging, not better hand hygiene or patient safety, and the only check that logging adds value is a rough ward rollout across three wards with only 30 sampled moments. The design also has no event history, version control or independent check of the kiosk data beyond the observers' tallies, and disputes are settled informally at huddles.

holistic.reason: The design is rigorous on verification, safeguards and fair measurement, but it is complex to run (audit sampling, a 30-moment minimum, a pause rule), and a ward-level meal is a weak, shared incentive that may not be noticed or sustain the habit once it ends.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never shows that kiosk logging is worth what it costs at the point of care or how it relates to infection outcomes, and its only adoption measure comes from the same observed audit sessions, where staff know they are being watched. The reward therefore pays for behaviour while observers are present, and the small three-ward stepped design with no stated uncertainty handling cannot reliably separate that effect from real adoption.

codex.worst_flaw: The core adoption measure is invalid for deciding whether to retain ward-wide logging because it counts only observer-verifiable actions and cannot distinguish routine logging from logging prompted by an observer’s presence.

holistic.reason: Safety-first design with pause triggers, audit-verified rewards, a staggered rollout and privacy protections is approvable, but a team meal is a weak, delayed motivator, observer verification and sample sizes are fiddly, and extra logging work for busy nurses may fade once the reward ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward and exit thresholds use a rate that counts tickets without a suitable or timely approved article, so differences in case mix and approval turnaround can determine which teams qualify and whether the pilot appears to succeed.

claude.worst_flaw: The pilot cannot separate the reward's effect from the workflow change: the cohort comparison covers only two weeks across a few teams with no uncertainty or spillover handling, the same weeks add the resolve-screen default, and the keep/change/drop decision uses absolute rate thresholds rather than incremental lift over plain support. The flat 50% personal goal also ignores small books and case mix where no suitable article exists.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with workflow fixes, QA and CSAT guardrails, a staged comparison, and a default-workflow handoff that supports persistence, but it is complex to administer for one owner in an hour a week and the 60% team threshold and anti-gaming checks add friction.

codex.worst_flaw: Customer-data leakage is a launch blocker because the QA rule can clear awards when two sampled tickets expose customer data and gives no procedure for containing the exposure.

claude.worst_flaw: The 50% target and the QA trigger (fewer than 8 of 10 passing) are not linked to any measured baseline. The plan also never checks whether the existing CSAT bonus pushes agents to skip or rush articles, and low-volume agents and uneven case mix across queues are barely handled.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with workflow fixes first, quality sampling, a randomized stagger, and an honest decision rule, but a single hour of PTO for a team goal is a modest incentive, the 50% target is a big jump from 12%, and lasting change depends mainly on the workflow fixes staying in place.

codex.worst_flaw: The same 50% reward threshold applies across teams regardless of how many tickets can safely use an article, so case mix can determine who earns the reward and create pressure to link unsuitable articles.

claude.worst_flaw: Pay still includes a CSAT bonus, yet nothing checks whether time spent on articles cuts into that bonus or pushes people to rush. The fixed 1-in-2 personal goal also ignores case mix. And audit tooling is thin: there is no replayable event history, no shadow validation and no staffed appeals process.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with sound measurement, guardrails, and workflow fixes, but a single paid hour off is a weak incentive, the rules are complex to communicate, and a team-level 50% target is ambitious from a 12% baseline, though removing friction should help the behaviour persist.
